prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which a magic-wavelength trap cancels the light shift and brought atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my single-part position, and the first round sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The chair asks what is discovered beyond better numbers. My answer in one sentence: Katori's insight that there is a wavelength at which a standing wave of light does not shift the clock transition, so that thousands of atoms can be held motionless and interrogated at once, was a new way to remove the dominant systematic of a quantum absorber, and once the budget reached 10^-18 the instrument became a probe that resolves the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, shows many-body interactions in a clock, and bounds drifts of constants. That is a change of what can be observed, and it is not a refinement of the comb or of ion trapping, which are tools the lattice clock uses rather than anticipates. The evidence is the kind I trust: independent reproduction at RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST, clock-to-clock comparisons that agree within the stated budgets, and no one arguing that the result is unverified. The attribution is two names, both named by every supporter. Following Danielsson, Kroll and Pearce, I would keep the pending redefinition of the second out of the citation and the rationale, and let the instrument and its physics carry it. On the priority question raised by Johansson and Kroll, my recollection is that Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme and demonstrated the Sr lattice clock in 2003 and onward, and that Ye's group made the leading accuracy and stability advances. I would still welcome a formal check of the record before the vote, since I have only my memory of it.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 1997, 2005, 2012 and 2018 prizes is real and I will not wave it away. Eriksson and Mehlig are right that part of this story is a patient programme of systematic-error reduction, and a reader could see the prize as rewarding the crossing of a precision threshold in a field already honoured. I think the magic-wavelength concept answers this, but it does not remove the risk that the citation is read as a prize for records. The credit is also not airtight: Lemonde at SYRTE, Derevianko and colleagues for the theory of magic wavelengths and shifts, the Ludlow-Hinkley teams and the single-ion groups sit outside two names, and a prize reaching the 10^-18 milestone could equally be argued as an instrument prize shared with ion-clock groups. Finally, I am an atomic theorist and the lattice clock sits near my own field, so I should apply to it the same demand for maturity and independent verification that I put to others. In particular, I have moved to treat Mehlig's low ranking as a serious signal, not an outlier.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether the committee sees a single decisive discovery in lattice clocks or an instrument that has crossed a threshold, and defers to me on whether 10^-18 is a physical discovery or a technical achievement.
responses.response: I would not call 10^-18 itself the discovery, and I do not want the citation to say so. The discovery is the magic-wavelength principle: a trap whose potential does not perturb the transition, which turned a long-standing trade-off between interrogation time and perturbation into something that no longer constrains the measurement. The 10^-18 level is the evidence that the principle works as an instrument, and it is also where new physics becomes visible, with many-body collisions and lattice-induced shifts appearing in the systematics. I admit that this is partly a matter of judgement about where invention ends and refinement begins. Where we may still differ is on weight. You value stability of interpretation most, and for that criterion the clock is as secure as the topological insulator: independent reproduction in several institutes with an agreed uncertainty budget. I read your own ranking of it as an alternative as consistent with that, and I would ask whether a narrow citation on the invention would answer your remaining concern.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from active matter to twisted bilayer graphene and ranked lattice clocks sixth because they look like a long incremental improvement of earlier metrology prizes, while arguing that B047 has theory-then-experiment structure and reproduction across many groups.
responses.response: I take the incremental objection seriously and I do not think it can be settled by counting prizes. My test is whether the instrument gave access to something that earlier tools did not. For clocks I believe it did: relativistic redshift across millimetres and many-body effects inside a clock are observations, not improvements of an old number. I do accept that this is less striking than a new phase of matter. On your configuration, I agree about the structure, a quantitative prediction followed by an experiment where it said to look, and I called it persuasive in round 1. What keeps me from moving is the point you list yourself, an unsettled pairing mechanism and the 2018 first authors outside the names. For atomic physics I would not award a prize while the central question about the new state is open, and I would ask you what you would accept as sufficient evidence of a stable interpretation. If the committee judges B047 mature enough, it is my first alternative and I would not obstruct it.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to lattice clocks, but pushes back on my round-1 second alternative B017 by saying quantum simulation has not yet delivered a decisive new result beyond quantum-gas microscopy, and asks for a check of the record on the priority of the first Sr lattice clock and on theory credit.
responses.response: Your criticism of B017 is fair and it changes my alternatives. The case for ultracold-atom simulation is real, but the credit is four names, which exceeds what a two-name clock could be combined with under the three-person limit, and I cannot name the single decisive result it delivered that the microscope and the Mott transition did not already show. I therefore move B017 to second alternative behind B047 and drop circuit QED, partly for the reasons you gave in round 1 about the 2025 prize and the transmon credit, partly because you will probably recuse on it. On the clock priority record I agree and would go further: Katori's 2003 proposal and Sr lattice demonstration, the JILA and SYRTE Sr work in 2005 to 2006, and Derevianko's magic-wavelength calculations should be checked against the record before the vote, though I am confident that the prize goes to the proposal and its realisation, not to the theory of shifts.

responses.point: Olsson keeps twisted bilayer graphene first because a number was predicted and then found, the central phenomena are reproduced in many laboratories, and waiting is not neutral, and has the clock only fourth.
responses.response: The prediction-then-observation structure is the most beautiful argument on the shortlist and I do not dismiss it. You have also answered my maturity point partly, since the correlated phases are seen widely. Two things still hold me back. First, the experimental credit for the 2018 result sits with first authors who cannot be named, so the three-name set would reward the group leader and the theorists for something the junior authors did. Second, the pairing mechanism is open, and I would want a stronger sign that the superconductivity is understood and robust against twist-angle disorder before awarding this. I do not consider that disqualifying, and for a platform discovery I can accept that the prize may have to precede the mechanism. If the committee becomes uneasy about the clock, B047 is the configuration I would move to, and I would then ask that the citation keep the prediction and the discovery together as you have worded it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, after weighing the 1997, 2005, 2012 and 2018 prizes, will accept the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a distinct achievement or as a continuation of precision spectroscopy; Mehlig's sixth place suggests this is not settled.

The priority record for the first Sr lattice clock, and whether Lemonde, Derevianko or other lattice-clock groups should weigh more heavily than I now judge; I am relying on recollection and have not verified the dates.

Whether a pairing mechanism for superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene will be resolved soon enough to change the maturity argument for B047, a field in which I defer to Mehlig, Olsson and Eriksson.

Whether the committee would prefer a two-part prize, for instance the clock with a condensed-matter discovery, over a single clean two-name part; I judge a single part clearer, but I have no strong view.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I am an atomic theorist and my own field is close to the lattice clock, so I may overvalue it, and I have tried to hold it to the same independence tests as other candidates. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (Lund, 2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and Keller (ETH) attosecond groups; none of them is on the shortlist. I have no known link to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or the B017 names. I am not aware of any change since round 1.
